items.titleEn: The Longest Bridge on the Road
items.bodyEn: Yahagi Bridge carried the Tōkaidō over the Yahagi River into Okazaki, a castle town and the birthplace of Tokugawa Ieyasu. At 208 ken, roughly 380 meters, it was the longest bridge on the whole highway. Hiroshige drew a daimyō procession filing across it, lances raised, with the keep of Okazaki Castle rising beyond the river.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Fifty-three Stations (Hōeidō ed.), Okazaki 'Yahagi no hashi'

items.bodyEn: 橋 joins 木, wood, to 喬, which means tall and arching and also lends the character its sound. The Shuowen Jiezi explains it plainly as a beam laid across water. Picture a high wooden span curving over a river, exactly what the Yahagi crossing was, and the two halves of the character fall into place.
items.sourceNote: Shuowen Jiezi, entry 橋 (水梁也、从木喬聲)

items.titleEn: くせに Blames, わりに Compares
items.bodyEn: Both くせに and わりに translate as 'although', but they feel very different. わりに neutrally weighs one fact against another: cheap for how good it is. くせに carries reproach and is aimed at someone who should have behaved better: they know, yet they will not tell you. Never use くせに about yourself or a superior; it sounds like an accusation.
items.ja: {知|し}っているくせに{教|おし}えてくれない。
items.kana: しっているくせにおしえてくれない。

items.bodyEn: Okazaki's dark, dense soybean miso is called Hatchō miso after Hatchō village, which stood eight chō, about 870 meters, west of Okazaki Castle. Brewers there aged the paste for two summers and more in huge cedar vats, each weighted down with a pyramid of river stones. The name still records a distance rather than a recipe.
items.sourceNote: Daijisen, entry 八丁味噌; Okazaki local history (Hatchō village)
